title: Ἡ ὁδὸς Τηλεμάχου
about: Telemachus renews before the assembly his request for a ship to seek news of his long-absent father; Mentor rebukes the people of Ithaca for their silence in the face of the suitors, and Leiocritus answers him with contempt before the assembly breaks up. Telemachus then prays alone by the shore, and Athena, disguised as Mentor, promises to fit out a ship and gather a crew herself; back at the house, Antinous mockingly offers to have the Achaeans see to the journey, and Telemachus refuses to stay silent among them any longer.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun 'him', not the article — in Homer the article of later Greek still functions mainly as a demonstrative or personal pronoun, a pattern to watch for throughout this part. This whole line is the house-fixed reply-formula for Telemachus, fixed by its earlier appearance at 2.208 in the published odyssey-004 and reused here unchanged; it recurs again at 2.309, later in this same part. πεπνυμένος, 'prudent', is properly the perfect participle of a verb meaning 'to have one's wits about one', and is Telemachus's fixed epithet throughout the poem. ἀντίον ηὔδα, '(he) spoke face to face', is ηὔδα, the (regularly augmented) imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak, utter'.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύμαχ’ ἠδὲ καὶ ἄλλοι, ὅσοι μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί,
ταῦτα μὲν οὐχ ὑμέας ἔτι λίσσομαι οὐδ’ ἀγορεύω·
sentences.l:
“Eurymachus, and you others too, as many as are the noble suitors,
this, at least, I no longer beg of you, nor argue it;
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, and the rest of you noble suitors, I no longer beg you about this, nor argue it any further;
sentences.n: ἀγαυοί, 'noble, illustrious', is a new stock epithet in this part (it returns at 2.247); its root is disputed, perhaps connected with ἄγαμαι 'wonder at, admire'. It is kept distinct here from ἀγανός 'gentle' at 2.230 and from the house-fixed ἀγήνωρ 'lordly' of μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες. λίσσομαι 'beg, entreat' and ἀγορεύω 'declare publicly' together recall Telemachus's earlier plea to the assembly; ταῦτα μέν, answered by ἀλλά in 2.212, marks his pivot from that old appeal to the new request that follows.

sentences.t: ἤδη γὰρ τὰ ἴσασι θεοὶ καὶ πάντες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l: for already the gods know these things, and all the Achaeans.
sentences.i: for the gods already know it, and all the Achaeans too.
sentences.n: τά is again the pronoun rather than the article, 'these things', object of ἴσασι, the perfect-with-present-force of οἶδα. Telemachus drops his earlier complaint on the ground that it is now common knowledge; the suitors' misconduct has already been aired before the whole assembly.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι δότε νῆα θοὴν καὶ εἴκοσ’ ἑταίρους,
οἵ κέ μοι ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα διαπρήσσωσι κέλευθον.
sentences.l:
But come, give me a swift ship and twenty companions,
who for me here and there may accomplish the way.
sentences.i: But come, give me a swift ship and twenty companions who will carry the journey through for me, this way and that.
sentences.n: ἄγε is an imperative used as an interjection, 'come now'; ἀλλ' ἄγε answers ταῦτα μέν of 2.210. ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα, literally 'here and there', is idiomatic for a voyage of more than one leg. διαπρήσσωσι, 'accomplish, carry through', governs κέλευθον, 'the way, the journey'; the subjunctive with κέ (= ἄν) expresses purpose.

sentences.t:
εἶμι γὰρ ἐς Σπάρτην τε καὶ ἐς Πύλον ἠμαθόεντα
νόστον πευσόμενος πατρὸς δὴν οἰχομένοιο,
ἤν τίς μοι εἴπῃσι βροτῶν ἢ ὄσσαν ἀκούσω
ἐκ Διός, ἥ τε μάλιστα φέρει κλέος ἀνθρώποισιν·
sentences.i: for I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos, to ask after the homecoming of my father, who has long been gone, in case some mortal may tell me of it, or I may hear a rumor sent from Zeus, which above all brings men report;
sentences.n: ἐς is the shorter epic form beside εἰς. Πύλον ἠμαθόεντα, 'sandy Pylos', is the house-fixed epithet. οἰχομένοιο is a genitive in -οιο (= Attic -ου), from οἴχομαι 'be gone', a present used with perfect force for a long absence; πατρὸς δὴν οἰχομένοιο returns unchanged at 2.264. ἀνθρώποισιν is a dative plural in -οισι(ν) (Attic -οις). ὄσσα, literally 'a voice', is a report or rumor sent by Zeus; later poets make her a goddess, but she stays a common noun here, matching Murray's lower case. ἥ τε, with the generalizing epic τε, extends the claim beyond this occasion. κλέος keeps its root sense 'report', not 'fame' — the identical formula is already published at 1.283 in odyssey-003, with the same gloss.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κεν πατρὸς βίοτον καὶ νόστον ἀκούσω,
ἦ τ’ ἄν, τρυχόμενός περ, ἔτι τλαίην ἐνιαυτόν·
sentences.l:
if indeed my father's life and homecoming I hear of,
then, worn though I am, I would yet endure a year;
sentences.i: if I hear that my father is alive and coming home, then, worn as I am, I would still hold out for another year;
sentences.n: βίοτον καὶ νόστον is close to a hendiadys, 'his life, that is, his living homecoming'. τρυχόμενός περ, 'worn out though I am', shows περ attached to a participle to give it concessive force, where Attic would use καίπερ. τλαίην is the optative of τλάω 'endure, bear', in a conclusion answering the conditional εἰ … ἀκούσω.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε τεθνηῶτος ἀκούσω μηδ’ ἔτ’ ἐόντος,
νοστήσας δὴ ἔπειτα φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
σῆμά τέ οἱ χεύω καὶ ἐπὶ κτέρεα κτερεΐξω
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσα ἔοικε, καὶ ἀνέρι μητέρα δώσω.
sentences.l:
but if I hear that he is dead and no longer living,
then, having returned to my dear fatherland,
I will heap up a mound for him, and pay funeral honours besides,
very many, as many as is fitting, and give my mother to a husband.”
sentences.i: but if I hear that he is dead and gone, then, once I have returned to my dear fatherland, I will heap up a mound for him and pay him funeral honours in full, as many as are fitting, and give my mother to a husband.”
sentences.n: This unit echoes closely, in a different person, the wording already fixed at 2.221 in the published odyssey-003 (there Athena, disguised as Mentes, advising Telemachus in the second person; here Telemachus himself in the first); the two passages share σῆμά τε … χεύω and κτέρεα κτερεΐξω but differ in mood and person, so they are not the identical unit the validator would force to match. ἐπί is adverbial here, 'besides, in addition', not tmesis with a following verb. μητέρα δώσω, 'I will give my mother [in marriage]', closes Telemachus's first speech of the part.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὅ γ’ ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο, τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη
Μέντωρ, ὅς ῥ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος ἦεν ἑταῖρος,
καί οἱ ἰὼν ἐν νηυσὶν ἐπέτρεπεν οἶκον ἅπαντα,
πείθεσθαί τε γέροντι καὶ ἔμπεδα πάντα φυλάσσειν·
sentences.l:
He then, having so spoken, sat down; and among them stood up
Mentor, who was the companion of blameless Odysseus,
and to him, going aboard the ships, he had entrusted his whole household,
to obey the old man and to keep all things steadfast;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down; and among them there stood up Mentor, who had been the companion of blameless Odysseus, and to whom, when he went aboard the ships, Odysseus had entrusted his whole household, to obey the old man and keep everything secure;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι marks a transition, 'well then, indeed'. κατ’ … ἕζετο is tmesis, the preverb κατά standing apart from ἕζετο (= κατέζετο); ἕζετο itself keeps its short initial vowel rather than lengthening it, another instance of the missing augment this poem shows throughout. ὅς ῥ(α) carries the particle ῥα, a worn-down ἄρα, very common after a relative or a name. ἀμύμονος is the stock epithet already met of Odysseus in odyssey-001 (1.29): its usual gloss 'blameless' is kept, though the word's real sense is not securely known. Mentor is introduced here for the only time before he lends his shape to Athena later in this same part.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν is the house-fixed formula for opening a speech to an assembly. ἐὺ φρονέων is the uncontracted present participle (Attic εὖ φρονῶν, 'thinking well, well disposed'); the uncontracted form recurs at 2.238 (νέεσθαι). σφιν is the enclitic dative plural, 'to/toward them'.

sentences.t: κέκλυτε δὴ νῦν μευ, Ἰθακήσιοι, ὅττι κεν εἴπω·
sentences.l: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca, whatever I may say;
sentences.i: “Hear me now, men of Ithaca, and hear what I have to say.
sentences.n: This whole line is fixed by its earlier appearance at 2.229 in the published odyssey-005, and its wording is reused here unchanged. κέκλυτε is the aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear', with the genitive μευ (= μου). ὅττι is the epic form of ὅ τι, 'whatever', with κεν (= ἄν) in a general or indefinite clause.

sentences.t:
μή τις ἔτι πρόφρων ἀγανὸς καὶ ἤπιος ἔστω
σκηπτοῦχος βασιλεύς, μηδὲ φρεσὶν αἴσιμα εἰδώς,
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ χαλεπός τ’ εἴη καὶ αἴσυλα ῥέζοι·
sentences.i: let no sceptred king any longer be ready-minded, gentle and kind, nor mindful of what is right — let him always be harsh and act wickedly instead —
sentences.n: πρόφρων, 'well-disposed, eager-minded', and ἤπιος, 'gentle, kind', together describe the ideal king Mentor says Ithaca will no longer have. σκηπτοῦχος βασιλεύς, 'the sceptre-holding king', is a formula built on σκῆπτρον. αἴσιμα … αἴσυλα plays on two look-alike but opposite adjectives, αἴσιμος 'fitting, right' and αἴσυλος 'presumptuous, wicked'. αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί.

sentences.t:
ὡς οὔ τις μέμνηται Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
λαῶν οἷσιν ἄνασσε, πατὴρ δ’ ὣς ἤπιος ἦεν.
sentences.l:
as no one remembers divine Odysseus
among the people whom he ruled — and like a father kind he was.
sentences.i: since no one remembers divine Odysseus, among the people he ruled — and was as gentle as a father.
sentences.n: θείοιο is a further genitive in -οιο, of θεῖος 'divine', an epithet Murray applies to Odysseus himself here, not only to Phemius as in the house table; it is kept to the same rendering, 'divine'. λαῶν οἷσιν ἄνασσε: οἷσιν here is the ordinary relative pronoun, dative plural, object of ἄνασσε ('was lord over'), not the look-alike possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν 'his own' that this form can be mistaken for. πατὴρ δ’ ὣς ἤπιος ἦεν is the house-fixed line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας οὔ τι μεγαίρω
ἔρδειν ἔργα βίαια κακορραφίῃσι νόοιο·
sentences.l:
But indeed the lordly suitors I do not at all grudge
for doing violent deeds through the evil devisings of their mind;
sentences.i: But it is not the lordly suitors' violent deeds, done through the evil scheming of their minds, that I grudge them —
sentences.n: μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας is the house-fixed epithet, 'the lordly suitors' (kept distinct from ἀγαυοί 'noble' at 2.209 and 2.247). μεγαίρω + infinitive is 'grudge, be unwilling to allow'; the sense only becomes clear with the νῦν δέ of 2.239, which turns from what Mentor does not grudge the suitors to what he does resent in the rest of the people. κακορραφίῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι(ν), instrumental, 'by their evil devisings' (κακός + ῥάπτω, 'contrive, stitch together').

sentences.t:
σφὰς γὰρ παρθέμενοι κεφαλὰς κατέδουσι βιαίως
οἶκον Ὀδυσσῆος, τὸν δ’ οὐκέτι φασὶ νέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
for staking their own heads, they violently devour
the house of Odysseus, and say that he no longer will return.
sentences.i: for, staking their own lives, they violently devour the house of Odysseus, and say that he will never come back.
sentences.n: παρθέμενοι, 'having staked, put at risk', is the aorist middle participle of παρατίθημι; σφὰς κεφαλάς, 'their own heads', is a vivid idiom for their own lives. νέεσθαι, 'to return', is again uncontracted (Attic νεῖσθαι), sharing its root with νόστος.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἄλλῳ δήμῳ νεμεσίζομαι, οἷον ἅπαντες
ἧσθ’ ἄνεῳ, ἀτὰρ οὔ τι καθαπτόμενοι ἐπέεσσι
παύρους μνηστῆρας καταπαύετε πολλοὶ ἐόντες.
sentences.l:
but now at another people I feel indignation, that you all
sit silent, yet in no way, accosting with words,
do you, being many, restrain the suitors, who are few.”
sentences.i: but now it is the rest of you I resent, that you all sit silent, and, many as you are, never speak up to check the suitors, who are few.”
sentences.n: νεμεσίζομαι + dative is 'feel righteous indignation at, resent'; the ἄλλῳ δήμῳ he now turns to is the assembled people at large, as against the suitors just excused. ἧσθ(ε) is 'you sit', ἄνεῳ 'silent, speechless'. καθαπτόμενοι ἐπέεσσι, 'accosting with words', is built on the same verb as the house-fixed καθαπτόμενος προσέειπεν, here without the finite verb of speech. πολλοὶ ἐόντες, 'though you are many', is a concessive participle; this closes Mentor's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Εὐηνορίδης Λειώκριτος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: Him then Leiocritus, son of Evenor, addressed, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Leiocritus, son of Evenor, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is a new variant of the reply-formula, on the pattern name + patronymic + ἀντίον ηὔδα already fixed for Eurymachus (τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρύμαχος Πολύβου πάϊς ἀντίον ηὔδα); its wording is logged in new-renderings.md for any future recurrence. Εὐηνορίδης, 'son of Evenor', is a patronymic adjective of the same formation as Ἀτρεΐδης 'son of Atreus'. Leiocritus is a suitor named nowhere else so far in the poem.

sentences.t:
Μέντορ ἀταρτηρέ, φρένας ἠλεέ, ποῖον ἔειπες
ἡμέας ὀτρύνων καταπαυέμεν.
sentences.l:
“Mentor, reckless one, distraught in your wits, what a thing you have said,
urging us to make an end;
sentences.i: “Mentor, you reckless man, out of your wits, what a thing to say, urging us to stop!
sentences.n: ἀταρτηρέ, 'reckless, mischievous', and φρένας ἠλεέ, 'crazed in your wits' (accusative of respect), are two insults in a row. ποῖον ἔειπες, 'what sort of thing have you said', is a reproach, like ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων in the pilot part. καταπαυέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (Attic καταπαύειν), the first of this type in the part; it depends on ὀτρύνων, 'urging'.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον δὲ
ἀνδράσι καὶ πλεόνεσσι μαχήσασθαι περὶ δαιτί.
sentences.l:
and it is a hard thing
for men, even greater numbers of them, to fight over a feast.
sentences.i: it is a hard thing for men to fight it out over a feast, even against greater numbers.
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον, 'hard, troublesome', governs the infinitive μαχήσασθαι. πλεόνεσσι is a dative plural comparative of πολύς, 'a greater number'; the same word recurs at 2.251 and is kept to the same rendering both times. περὶ δαιτί shows anastrophe, the accent of περί drawn back because it follows its noun: 'over, for the sake of, a feast'.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ κ’ Ὀδυσεὺς Ἰθακήσιος αὐτὸς ἐπελθὼν
δαινυμένους κατὰ δῶμα ἑὸν μνηστῆρας ἀγαυοὺς
ἐξελάσαι μεγάροιο μενοινήσει’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
sentences.l:
For even if Odysseus of Ithaca himself, coming upon them,
should set his heart, feasting throughout his own hall, the noble suitors,
to drive them out of the megaron,
sentences.i: For even if Odysseus of Ithaca himself should come upon the noble suitors feasting in his own hall, and should set his heart on driving them out of the great room,
sentences.n: εἴ περ … κ(ε) is a strongly concessive 'even if'. δῶμα ἑὸν uses ἑός, a byform of the reflexive possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν noted in conventions.md, 'his own'; this is the first instance of that possessive in this part. μενοινήσειε is an aorist optative, 'should set his heart on', governing the infinitive ἐξελάσαι; μεγάροιο is a genitive of separation, 'out of the hall'.

sentences.t:
οὔ κέν οἱ κεχάροιτο γυνή, μάλα περ χατέουσα,
ἐλθόντ’, ἀλλά κεν αὐτοῦ ἀεικέα πότμον ἐπίσποι,
εἰ πλεόνεσσι μάχοιτο·
sentences.i: not even then would his wife rejoice at his arrival, much as she longs for it — instead he would meet an unseemly end there, if he fought against superior numbers;
sentences.n: μάλα περ χατέουσα, 'longing for it very much though she is', pairs περ with a participle again, as at 2.219. ἐπίσποι is the aorist optative of ἐπισπεῖν, 'follow upon, meet with'; ἀεικέα πότμον is 'an unseemly fate'. πλεόνεσσι repeats 2.245 and is kept to the same rendering, 'greater numbers'.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ οὐ κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.l: But you have not spoken according to what is fitting.
sentences.i: but what you have said is not according to what is fitting.
sentences.n: κατὰ μοῖραν, 'according to due share, fittingly', is a common idiom for correct speech or action; οὐ κατὰ μοῖραν negates it, 'not as is proper'. This closes Leiocritus's rebuttal of Mentor's specific claim and turns, with ἀλλά in 2.252, to practical instructions.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε, λαοὶ μὲν σκίδνασθ’ ἐπὶ ἔργα ἕκαστος,
τούτῳ δ’ ὀτρυνέει Μέντωρ ὁδὸν ἠδ’ Ἁλιθέρσης,
οἵ τέ οἱ ἐξ ἀρχῆς πατρώιοί εἰσιν ἑταῖροι.
sentences.l:
But come, let the people scatter, each to his own tasks,
but for him Mentor will speed the way, and Halitherses,
who from the beginning are his father's own companions.
sentences.i: But come, let the people disperse, each to his own tasks; as for the journey, Mentor and Halitherses will see to it — they who have been his father's companions from the start.
sentences.n: σκίδνασθ(ε) is an imperative, distributed by the following ἕκαστος. ὀτρυνέει is a future in -έει (uncontracted, Attic ὀτρυνεῖ). πατρώιοί … ἑταῖροι, 'companions from his father's day', echoes the house-fixed πατρώιος ξεῖνος and is logged in new-renderings.md, since the same phrase, of the same two men, returns at 2.286 in this very part.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὀίω, καὶ δηθὰ καθήμενος ἀγγελιάων
πεύσεται εἰν Ἰθάκῃ, τελέει δ’ ὁδὸν οὔ ποτε ταύτην.
sentences.l:
But I think that, even sitting a long while for tidings,
he will learn them in Ithaca, and never accomplish this journey.”
sentences.i: But I expect that, even after sitting a long while waiting for news, he will get it right here in Ithaca, and never make this journey at all.”
sentences.n: ἀγγελιάων is an Ionic form with an uncontracted genitive plural ending -άων (Attic ἀγγελιῶν); the noun itself, ἀγγελίη 'message, tidings', shows the Ionic η where Attic keeps long α. δηθὰ καθήμενος, 'sitting for a long while', is Leiocritus's sneer: Telemachus will get his news without ever leaving home. This closes his speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, λῦσεν δ’ ἀγορὴν αἰψηρήν.
sentences.l: So then he declared, and dissolved the hasty assembly.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and broke up the hastily-gathered assembly.
sentences.n: ἐφώνησεν is the aorist of φωνέω, 'utter, give voice to'. αἰψηρήν, 'hasty', describes the assembly itself, called on short notice at the start of this book.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐσκίδναντο ἑὰ πρὸς δώμαθ’ ἕκαστος,
μνηστῆρες δ’ ἐς δώματ’ ἴσαν θείου Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l:
They, then, scattered, each to his own home,
but the suitors went to the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.i: The people scattered, each to his own home, but the suitors went off to the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἑὰ … ἕκαστος is again the possessive ἑός, 'his own', neuter plural with δώματα understood. θείου Ὀδυσῆος, 'of divine Odysseus', uses θεῖος in its ordinary generic sense (kept to 'divine' throughout, as already fixed for Phemius); it is not the same word as δῖος, kept to 'heavenly' when it describes Odysseus elsewhere.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἀπάνευθε κιὼν ἐπὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης,
χεῖρας νιψάμενος πολιῆς ἁλὸς εὔχετ’ Ἀθήνῃ·
sentences.l:
But Telemachus, going apart, to the shore of the sea,
having washed his hands in the grey sea, prayed to Athena:
sentences.i: But Telemachus went off by himself to the shore of the sea, and, having washed his hands in the grey sea, prayed to Athena:
sentences.n: ἀπάνευθε κιών, 'going off apart', sets Telemachus alone against the crowd just dispersed. πολιῆς ἁλός, 'of the grey sea', is a new fixed epithet, logged in new-renderings.md, since πολιός is a common Homeric colour-word for the sea and is likely to return. νιψάμενος is the aorist middle participle of νίζω, 'wash'; ritual washing regularly precedes a prayer in Homer.

sentences.t:
κλῦθί μευ, ὃ χθιζὸς θεὸς ἤλυθες ἡμέτερον δῶ
καί μ’ ἐν νηὶ κέλευσας ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον
νόστον πευσόμενον πατρὸς δὴν οἰχομένοιο
ἔρχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
“Hear me, you who yesterday, a god, came to our house
and bade me, in a ship, over the misty-looking sea,
of my father's homecoming to inquire, long gone,
to go —
sentences.i: “Hear me, you who came to our house yesterday as a god, and bade me go by ship over the misty-looking sea to seek word of the homecoming of my father, who has long been gone —
sentences.n: χθιζὸς θεός, 'a god, but yesterday', recalls the disguised Athena's earlier visit to Telemachus, narrated in book 1. ἠεροειδέα πόντον, 'the misty-looking sea', is a further formula logged in new-renderings.md. πατρὸς δὴν οἰχομένοιο repeats 2.215 exactly and is kept to the same wording. ἔρχεσθαι stands last, its infinitive depending on κέλευσας two lines above; the sentence ends mid-line, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τὰ δὲ πάντα διατρίβουσιν Ἀχαιοί,
μνηστῆρες δὲ μάλιστα κακῶς ὑπερηνορέοντες.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans obstruct all this,
and the suitors most of all, wickedly overbearing.”
sentences.i: but the Achaeans are putting off all of that, and the suitors most of all, in their wicked arrogance.”
sentences.n: διατρίβουσιν, 'wear away the time over, obstruct', takes τὰ πάντα as its object, 'all these things', i.e. the journey just described. ὑπερηνορέοντες, 'being overbearing, presumptuous' (built on the same root as ἀγήνωρ), closes the prayer with the suitors squarely blamed.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ ἦλθεν Ἀθήνη,
Μέντορι εἰδομένη ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ αὐδήν,
καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, praying, and near at hand came to him Athena,
likened to Mentor, both in body and in voice,
and, lifting her voice, to him winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Athena came close to him, having taken the shape of Mentor, in body and in voice alike, and, raising her voice, spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: εὐχόμενος, 'praying', names what the preceding speech was. Μέντορι εἰδομένη, 'having made herself like Mentor', uses the aorist participle of εἴδομαι, 'seem like, take on the appearance of' + dative; this is the disguise the goddess keeps for the rest of the part. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the house-fixed formula, 'winged words she spoke' (Attic third person; already published with 'he' at 1.122 in odyssey-002, adapted here to the goddess's own gender, φωνήσασ' feminine where φωνήσας was masculine there).

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, οὐδ’ ὄπιθεν κακὸς ἔσσεαι οὐδ’ ἀνοήμων,
εἰ δή τοι σοῦ πατρὸς ἐνέστακται μένος ἠύ,
οἷος κεῖνος ἔην τελέσαι ἔργον τε ἔπος τε·
sentences.i: “Telemachus, you will not be a base man hereafter, nor a witless one, if indeed your father's noble spirit has truly been instilled in you — such a man was he at bringing both deed and word to fulfillment;
sentences.n: ὄπιθεν, 'hereafter, in time to come' (literally 'from behind'), is built with the directional suffix -θεν, like -δε and -θι. ἐνέστακται is a perfect passive, 'has been instilled, dripped into [you]' (ἐνστάζω). This whole clause, οὐδ’ ὄπιθεν κακὸς ἔσσεαι οὐδ’ ἀνοήμων, returns verbatim at 2.278 and is kept to the same English both times.

sentences.t: οὔ τοι ἔπειθ’ ἁλίη ὁδὸς ἔσσεται οὐδ’ ἀτέλεστος.
sentences.l: then your journey will not thereafter be fruitless, nor unaccomplished.
sentences.i: then your journey will not be a fruitless one, or go unfulfilled.
sentences.n: ἁλίη, 'fruitless, vain', happens to look like a derivative of ἅλς 'sea' but is in fact unrelated, from ἅλιος 'in vain'; the same word recurs at 2.318 and is kept to the same rendering there.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ οὐ κείνου γ’ ἐσσὶ γόνος καὶ Πηνελοπείης,
οὐ σέ γ’ ἔπειτα ἔολπα τελευτήσειν, ἃ μενοινᾷς.
sentences.l:
but if you are not, then, the offspring of that man and of Penelope,
I do not then expect that you will accomplish what you desire.
sentences.i: but if you are not truly the son of that man and of Penelope, then I do not expect that you will accomplish what you have set your heart on.
sentences.n: κείνου is ἐκείνου. ἔολπα is a reduplicated perfect with present force, 'I hope, expect' (from ἔλπω); μενοινᾷς, 'you set your heart on, desire eagerly', recurs at 2.285.

sentences.t:
παῦροι γάρ τοι παῖδες ὁμοῖοι πατρὶ πέλονται,
οἱ πλέονες κακίους, παῦροι δέ τε πατρὸς ἀρείους.
sentences.l:
for few indeed are the sons who prove like their father,
the most part worse, and few indeed better than their father.
sentences.i: for few sons indeed turn out like their fathers — most are worse, and only a few better than their father.
sentences.n: πέλονται, 'prove to be, turn out', is a common epic equivalent of εἰσί with a more dynamic sense. κακίους and ἀρείους are comparatives of κακός and ἀγαθός (the latter irregular, from ἀρείων); the epic τε in παῦροι δέ τε marks this as a general truth about fathers and sons, not only about Telemachus.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ οὐδ’ ὄπιθεν κακὸς ἔσσεαι οὐδ’ ἀνοήμων,
οὐδέ σε πάγχυ γε μῆτις Ὀδυσσῆος προλέλοιπεν,
ἐλπωρή τοι ἔπειτα τελευτῆσαι τάδε ἔργα.
sentences.l:
But since not hereafter will you be base, nor witless,
nor has the cunning of Odysseus altogether forsaken you,
there is hope, then, that you will accomplish these deeds.
sentences.i: But since you will not be a base man hereafter, nor a witless one, and Odysseus's cunning has not altogether deserted you, there is good hope that you will bring these things to pass.
sentences.n: The first line repeats 2.270 exactly and keeps the same English. πάγχυ, 'utterly, altogether', strengthens the negative; προλέλοιπεν is a perfect of προλείπω, 'abandon, forsake in advance'. μῆτις, 'cunning intelligence, craft', is the noun behind the house-fixed epithet πολύμητις; here it names Odysseus's own quality, passed to his son.

sentences.t:
τῶ νῦν μνηστήρων μὲν ἔα βουλήν τε νόον τε
ἀφραδέων, ἐπεὶ οὔ τι νοήμονες οὐδὲ δίκαιοι·
sentences.l:
Therefore now leave alone the plan and purpose of the suitors,
senseless as they are, since they are neither sensible nor just;
sentences.i: So now pay no heed to the plans and purposes of the suitors, senseless men that they are, since they are neither sensible nor just;
sentences.n: τῶ, 'therefore, wherefore', is the pronoun used adverbially (= τῷ). ἔα is the present imperative of ἐάω, 'let be, leave alone'. ἀφραδέων, 'senseless', is a genitive plural agreeing with μνηστήρων, held over to the start of its own line for emphasis.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι ἴσασιν θάνατον καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν,
ὃς δή σφι σχεδόν ἐστιν, ἐπ’ ἤματι πάντας ὀλέσθαι.
sentences.l:
nor do they know at all of death and black doom,
which indeed is close upon them, that on a single day they will all perish.
sentences.i: they have no idea at all of the death and black doom that is now close upon them, that on a single day they will all perish.
sentences.n: κῆρα μέλαιναν, 'black doom', personifies death as an agent that comes for a man; σφι is the enclitic dative plural, 'for them'. ἐπ’ ἤματι, 'in a day', with πάντας ὀλέσθαι (aorist infinitive of ὄλλυμι), foretells the suitors' slaughter to come.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ὁδὸς οὐκέτι δηρὸν ἀπέσσεται ἣν σὺ μενοινᾷς·
sentences.l: But for you the way you desire will not much longer be delayed;
sentences.i: But the journey you long for will not be delayed much longer for you now;
sentences.n: ἀπέσσεται is the future of ἄπειμι, 'be absent, be away'; here 'will be far off, delayed'. μενοινᾷς repeats 2.275 and is kept to the same rendering, 'desire'.

sentences.t:
τοῖος γάρ τοι ἑταῖρος ἐγὼ πατρώιός εἰμι,
ὅς τοι νῆα θοὴν στελέω καὶ ἅμ’ ἕψομαι αὐτός.
sentences.l:
for such a companion, from your father's day, am I to you,
who will fit out for you a swift ship, and myself go along.
sentences.i: for I am to you just such a companion of your father's day, one who will fit out a swift ship for you and go along with you myself.
sentences.n: ἑταῖρος ἐγὼ πατρώιος reuses the phrase already fixed at 2.254, πατρώιοί … ἑταῖροι, 'companions from his father's day', now in the singular of Mentor himself; the same rendering is kept. στελέω is a future of στέλλω, 'fit out, equip'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν πρὸς δώματ’ ἰὼν μνηστῆρσιν ὁμίλει,
ὅπλισσόν τ’ ἤια καὶ ἄγγεσιν ἄρσον ἅπαντα,
οἶνον ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσι, καὶ ἄλφιτα, μυελὸν ἀνδρῶν,
δέρμασιν ἐν πυκινοῖσιν·
sentences.l:
But you, going to the house, mingle with the suitors,
prepare provisions, and in vessels fit everything,
wine in two-handled jars, and barley-meal, the marrow of men,
in close-packed skins;
sentences.i: But you, go back to the house and mix with the suitors, get provisions ready, and pack everything into containers — wine in two-handled jars, and barley-meal, the marrow of men, in tightly-stitched skins;
sentences.n: ὁμίλει + dative is 'keep company with, mingle among'; Athena tells Telemachus to keep up appearances while the preparations are made behind the suitors' backs. ἤια, 'provisions for a journey', and ἄγγεσιν, 'in vessels, jars', with ἄρσον (aorist imperative of ἀραρίσκω, 'fit, arrange'), give the practical list that follows. μυελὸν ἀνδρῶν, 'the marrow of men', is a striking metaphor for barley-meal as the very stuff that sustains life.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἀνὰ δῆμον ἑταίρους
αἶψ’ ἐθελοντῆρας συλλέξομαι.
sentences.l:
and I, throughout the district, companions,
quickly, volunteers, will gather;
sentences.i: and I will quickly gather companions from around the district, men willing to come;
sentences.n: ἀνὰ δῆμον, 'throughout the district', marks the area of Athena's search, not the object of a verb of motion. ἐθελοντῆρας, 'volunteers, willing men', is the object of συλλέξομαι, 'I will gather together'.

sentences.t:
εἰσὶ δὲ νῆες
πολλαὶ ἐν ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ, νέαι ἠδὲ παλαιαί·
sentences.l:
and there are ships,
many in sea-girt Ithaca, both new and old;
sentences.i: there are ships enough — many of them in sea-girt Ithaca, both new and old;
sentences.n: ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ is the house-fixed epithet, 'sea-girt Ithaca' (ἀμφί 'around' + ἅλς 'sea'). νέαι ἠδὲ παλαιαί, 'new and old', assures Telemachus that a suitable ship is readily at hand.

sentences.t:
τάων μέν τοι ἐγὼν ἐπιόψομαι ἥ τις ἀρίστη,
ὦκα δ’ ἐφοπλίσσαντες ἐνήσομεν εὐρέι πόντῳ.
sentences.l:
of these, for you, I myself will look out which is the best,
and quickly, having equipped her, we will launch her on the broad sea.”
sentences.i: of these I will pick out for you whichever is best, and quickly, once we have fitted her out, we will launch her on the broad sea.”
sentences.n: ἐπιόψομαι, future of ἐφοράω, is 'look over, single out'. ἐφοπλίσσαντες, 'having fully equipped', and ἐνήσομεν, future of ἐνίημι, 'send/launch into' + dative, close Athena's speech, and with it her promise to do the practical work herself.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διός·
sentences.l: So spoke Athena, daughter of Zeus;
sentences.i: So spoke Athena, daughter of Zeus,
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διός is a new narrator's formula, on the pattern of the house-fixed ὣς φάτο but filled out with the goddess's name and patronymic; it is logged in new-renderings.md against its likely return. φάτ(ο), unlike ἔφατ’ at 2.267, drops the augment, another instance of the missing augment noted throughout this poem.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δὴν
Τηλέμαχος παρέμιμνεν, ἐπεὶ θεοῦ ἔκλυεν αὐδήν.
sentences.l:
and no longer any more did
Telemachus linger, since he had heard the voice of the god.
sentences.i: and Telemachus did not linger any longer, since he had heard the voice of the god.
sentences.n: παρέμιμνεν, 'stayed beside, lingered', is an imperfect of παραμίμνω. θεοῦ ἔκλυεν αὐδήν, 'heard the voice of the god', takes the genitive with a verb of hearing; Telemachus still thinks he has heard a god, not yet knowing it was Athena in Mentor's shape.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι πρὸς δῶμα, φίλον τετιημένος ἦτορ,
εὗρε δ’ ἄρα μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας ἐν μεγάροισιν,
αἶγας ἀνιεμένους σιάλους θ’ εὕοντας ἐν αὐλῇ.
sentences.l:
He set out to go toward the house, grieving in his own heart,
and found the lordly suitors in the halls,
goats being driven in, and fat hogs being singed, in the courtyard.
sentences.i: He set out for the house, grieving in his heart, and found the lordly suitors in the halls, and, in the courtyard, goats being driven in and fat hogs being singed.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, 'he set out to go', is the house-fixed formula (elsewhere βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν), built on βῆ, the unaugmented root aorist of βαίνω (Attic ἔβη). τετιημένος, 'grieved, distressed', is a perfect participle confined to this participial form. μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας is again the house-fixed 'the lordly suitors'. ἀνιεμένους (pres. mid./pass. part. of ἀνίημι, 'send up, let go, release') does not mean 'singe' — that sense belongs only to εὕοντας, from εὕω 'singe off the hair or bristles'. Here it describes goats driven into the courtyard, presumably for slaughter, while the hogs beside them are singed for roasting: two distinct actions of feast preparation, not one named twice.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἰθὺς γελάσας κίε Τηλεμάχοιο,
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l:
But Antinous, laughing outright, went straight for Telemachus,
and clasped him by the hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: But Antinous, with a straight-out laugh, went right up to Telemachus, took his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: This whole two-line approach is a new formula, logged in new-renderings.md against its likely return: the mocking Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἰθὺς γελάσας κίε Τηλεμάχοιο, then the hand-clasp and address. ἔν … φῦ is tmesis, the preverb ἐν separated from φῦ (aorist of φύω, 'grew [into], took firm hold'), an idiom for gripping someone's hand; ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε is a second tmesis, of ἐξονομάζω 'call by name, address directly'.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’ ὑψαγόρη, μένος ἄσχετε, μή τί τοι ἄλλο
ἐν στήθεσσι κακὸν μελέτω ἔργον τε ἔπος τε,
ἀλλά μοι ἐσθιέμεν καὶ πινέμεν, ὡς τὸ πάρος περ.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, lofty-talker, unrestrained-in-fury, let no other
evil deed or word be a care to you in your breast,
but rather eat, for me, and drink, just as before.
sentences.i: “Telemachus, you lofty talker, unrestrained in your fury, let no other evil deed or word trouble your heart — just eat and drink, as you did before.
sentences.n: Τηλέμαχ’ ὑψαγόρη, μένος ἄσχετε follows the wording already fixed at 2.85 in odyssey-005 for this same vocative address, kept for consistency within this group of occurrences (the near-miss at 1.385 uses a slightly different construction and is left as its own case, per QUESTIONS.md). μελέτω is a third-person imperative of μέλω, 'be a care to'. ἐσθιέμεν and πινέμεν are two more infinitives in -έμεν used as imperatives, like καταπαυέμεν at 2.244.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δέ τοι μάλα πάντα τελευτήσουσιν Ἀχαιοί,
νῆα καὶ ἐξαίτους ἐρέτας, ἵνα θᾶσσον ἵκηαι
ἐς Πύλον ἠγαθέην μετ’ ἀγαυοῦ πατρὸς ἀκουήν.
sentences.l:
And all these things the Achaeans will duly bring to pass for you,
a ship and picked-out oarsmen, so that the sooner you may come
to very sacred Pylos, after tidings of your noble father.”
sentences.i: The Achaeans will see to all of that for you — a ship and chosen oarsmen, so that you may reach very sacred Pylos all the sooner, in search of news of your noble father.”
sentences.n: ἐξαίτους, 'picked out, chosen', modifies ἐρέτας. ἠγαθέην, 'very sacred', is an intensive compound with ἀγα-. ἀκουήν, 'report, tidings', with the genitive πατρός, closes Antinous's speech with a mocking promise that stands in ironic contrast to Leiocritus's own words, two speeches earlier, that Telemachus would never make this journey at all (2.255–256).

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This line repeats 2.208 exactly, and, as there, its wording is fixed by its earlier appearance in the published odyssey-004; it will not recur again within this part.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνο’, οὔ πως ἔστιν ὑπερφιάλοισι μεθ’ ὑμῖν
δαίνυσθαί τ’ ἀκέοντα καὶ εὐφραίνεσθαι ἕκηλον.
sentences.l:
“Antinous, it is in no way possible, among you overweening men,
to feast in silence and to make merry at my ease.
sentences.i: “Antinous, there is no way I can feast among you overweening men in silence and enjoy myself in peace.
sentences.n: ὑπερφιάλοισι, 'overweening, arrogant', is dative plural, describing the suitors themselves. ἀκέοντα, 'silent', and ἕκηλον, 'at ease, undisturbed', are both accusative, agreeing with the unexpressed subject of the infinitives δαίνυσθαι and εὐφραίνεσθαι — Telemachus himself.

sentences.t:
ἦ οὐχ ἅλις ὡς τὸ πάροιθεν ἐκείρετε πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλὰ
κτήματ’ ἐμά, μνηστῆρες, ἐγὼ δ’ ἔτι νήπιος ἦα;
sentences.l:
Is it not enough that, as before, you shorn away many good things,
my possessions, suitors, while I was still a child?
sentences.i: Is it not enough that before now you stripped away so many good possessions of mine, suitors, while I was still a child?
sentences.n: ἐκείρετε, imperfect of κείρω, 'shear, cut down', here 'consume, waste away'; the same verb names shearing sheep, and is applied bitterly to the suitors' feasting on Telemachus's flocks. νήπιος, 'infant, still a child, witless', names his former helplessness; the line ends with the Greek question mark, the only one in this part.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὅτε δὴ μέγας εἰμὶ καὶ ἄλλων μῦθον ἀκούων
πυνθάνομαι, καὶ δή μοι ἀέξεται ἔνδοθι θυμός,
πειρήσω, ὥς κ’ ὔμμι κακὰς ἐπὶ κῆρας ἰήλω,
ἠὲ Πύλονδ’ ἐλθών, ἢ αὐτοῦ τῷδ’ ἐνὶ δήμῳ.
sentences.l:
But now, when I am grown, and hearing the speech of others
I come to understand, and indeed my spirit grows within me,
I will make trial, how upon you I may send evil fates,
whether by going to Pylos, or right here in this land.
sentences.i: But now that I am grown, and, by listening to what others say, I am learning, and my spirit is indeed growing within me, I will make the attempt to bring evil fates down on you, whether by going to Pylos, or right here in this land.
sentences.n: πυνθάνομαι, 'learn by inquiry, come to understand', governs the participle ἀκούων. ἀέξεται, 'grows, increases', describes his θυμός swelling with new confidence. ἰήλω is an aorist subjunctive of ἰάλλω, 'send, let fly'; κακὰς … κῆρας, 'evil death-spirits, fates', is the same κήρ already met at 2.283. Πύλονδ(ε) carries the directional suffix -δε, like ὄπιθεν's -θεν at 2.270.

sentences.t:
εἶμι μέν, οὐδ’ ἁλίη ὁδὸς ἔσσεται ἣν ἀγορεύω,
ἔμπορος·
sentences.l:
Go I will, and it will not be a fruitless journey that I speak of,
as a passenger;
sentences.i: I will go, and the journey I speak of will not be fruitless — I will go as a passenger;
sentences.n: ἁλίη repeats 2.273 and is kept to the same rendering, 'fruitless'. ἔμπορος, 'a passenger, one who travels by ship without owning it or rowing it', prepares for the clarification that follows: Telemachus has neither ship nor crew of his own.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ νηὸς ἐπήβολος οὐδ’ ἐρετάων
γίγνομαι·
sentences.l:
for of a ship I am not the master, nor of rowers
do I become one;
sentences.i: for I have no ship of my own, and no crew of rowers either;
sentences.n: ἐπήβολος + genitive, 'having a share of, master of', is confined to this fixed idiom of ownership. γίγνομαι here means little more than 'am', with the negative applying to both nouns, ship and rowers alike.

sentences.t: ὥς νύ που ὔμμιν ἐείσατο κέρδιον εἶναι.
sentences.l: since, I suppose, this seemed to you the more profitable course.”
sentences.i: since I suppose this seemed to you the more profitable thing.”
sentences.n: ἐείσατο is the aorist of εἴδομαι, 'seem, appear'; νύ που, 'I suppose, no doubt', is wry rather than genuinely uncertain. κέρδιον, a comparative of κέρδος 'gain, profit', closes the part on a note of bitter irony: the suitors, Telemachus implies, have kept him shipless on purpose, to their own advantage.
